RECOMMENDED RULINGS,
FINDINGS OF FACT,
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW,
AND PROPOSED ORDER
A hearing was held before Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Julie D. Reading on February 8, 2018, in Medford, Oregon. The record closed on April 9, 2018, following receipt of the parties’ post-hearing briefs.
Margaret Kirschnick, Attorney at Law, Tedesco Law Group, Portland, Oregon, represented Petitioner.
Diana Moffat, Local Government Law Group, Eugene, Oregon, represented Respondent.
__________________________________
On October 18, 2017, the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Local 223 (Petitioner) filed a unit clarification petition (Petition) to determine whether the City of Medford (City) should include the newly created Fleet Services Coordinator position in the bargaining unit. The City filed timely objections.
The issues are:
1. Is the Fleet Services Coordinator statutorily excluded from the existing unit as a supervisory employee?
2. Is the Fleet Services Coordinator included in the bargaining unit based on the collective bargaining agreement? 3
We conclude that the Fleet Services Coordinator is not a supervisor and is therefore included in the bargaining unit by statute. The parties’ collective bargaining agreement does not otherwise compel exclusion from the unit.
RULINGS
The rulings of the ALJ were reviewed and are correct.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The Parties
1. Petitioner is a labor organization within the meaning of ORS 243.650(13).
2. The City is a public employer within the meaning of ORS 243.650(20).
3. The City’s Public Works Department is in charge of managing the City’s utilities – such as sewer, street lighting, traffic signals, and storm drains. Within the Public Works Department is Fleet Services, which services all motorized vehicles and equipment utilized by the City as well as some external agencies.
4. The City started contracting with external agencies in 2007, which has increased the workload. At the time of the hearing, mechanical work was being performed by five Fleet Services Mechanics. They are all certified mechanics. However, they have varying strengths and weaknesses in different skill areas depending on their experience.
5. The Department of Public Works is overseen by the Director of Public Works. The Deputy Director of Public Works in Charge of Operations reports to the Director, and the Support Services Manager of Public Works reports to the Deputy Director. The Support Services Manager supervises Fleet Services.
6. Non-supervisory employees in the Public Works Department are represented by Petitioner. The parties’ employment relationship is governed by the Employment Relations Agreement between the City of Medford, Oregon and Teamsters Local Union No. 223 Representing Medford Municipal Mechanics (Agreement). The Agreement’s effective dates were July 1, 2014 through June 30, 2018.
7. The Agreement’s recognition clause states:
“2.1 Recognition - The City recognizes Teamsters Local Union No. 223 as the exclusive bargaining agent for all non-excluded employees in covered classifications in the Public Works Department. Classifications in the bargaining unit include Auto Service Worker, Fleet Services Mechanic and Fleet Services Mechanic, Senior.
2.2 Excluded Employees - Part-time, temporary, supervisory and confidential employees are excluded from the bargaining unit. Part-time employees are those who work less than forty (40) hours per week. Temporary employees are those who 4
are hired for a limited period of time not to exceed six (6) consecutive months from date of employment in a twelve (12) month period.
2.3 New Classifications - The City has the exclusive right to develop new classifications within the current organizational scope of this bargaining unit and adopt wage scales for those classifications. The City shall forward the new position classification specification and hourly wage schedule to the Union for its review. If the Union disagrees with the proposed wage scale for this new classification, the Union may reopen this Agreement for negotiations of only that new hourly wage scale for that new classification under the scope of this Agreement.” (Exh. R-1 at 5, emphasis added.)
8. At some point after the negotiation and ratification of the Agreement, the Auto Services Worker position was eliminated. Additionally, in 2016, the individual serving as the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior left the position and was not replaced.
9. The City had summarized Fleet Services Mechanic Senior’s job description as follows:
“[u]nder general supervision of the Support Services Manager, the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior is responsible for performing maintenance and repairs of fleet vehicles and equipment, including cars, construction equipment, emergency apparatus, light, medium and heavy trucks and all other equipment for the City of Medford Fleet Services Division. This position is distinguished from the Fleet Services Mechanic by its responsibility for performing lead work and fleet shop administrative tasks. May supervise other assigned staff.” (Exh. P-6 at 1.)
10. The Fleet Services Mechanic Senior had spent the majority of his time generating work orders; providing and maintaining accurate maintenance records; estimating the labor, material and equipment necessary to complete assignments; directing and instructing other employees; and providing administrative duties as necessary for efficient operations. The remaining amount of time was spent directly working on vehicles. A mechanic certification was required for the position.
11. Shortly, after the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior position was vacated, the City created the Fleet Services Coordinator position. The City created it because the increased workload from external agencies required someone in a position to frequently interact with the customers and coordinate mechanical tasks.
12. The Fleet Services Coordinator position assumed most of the duties of the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior position with the exception of direct mechanical work. In place of mechanical work, some duties previously performed by the Support Services Manager were assigned to the Fleet Services Coordinator position.
13. Fleet Services Coordinator’s job description summary is: “[u]nder general supervision of the Support Services Manager, the Fleet Services [C]oordinator is responsible for coordinating, prioritizing, and scheduling the service and repair of fleet vehicles and equipment, 5
including cars, construction equipment, emergency apparatus, light, medium and heavy trucks and all other equipment for the City of Medford Fleet Services Division.” (Exh. R-3 at 1.)
14. The Fleet Services Coordinator’s primary duties are to essentially maintain a schedule of needed maintenance and inspections, keep necessary supplies stocked, accept repair requests, and then dispatch Fleet Services Mechanics to perform the needed work – determining prioritization and considering the relative strengths of the mechanics. The Fleet Services Coordinator also makes ongoing entries into City databases of vehicles, equipment, gas cards, and purchase orders. As such, the Fleet Services Coordinator’s duties could otherwise be described as scheduling, planning, coordinating, and assigning repair work; coordinating state and federal mandated inspections; establishing and maintaining maintenance records; authorizing the purchase of parts, equipment and supplies; reviewing completed work orders to ensure accuracy; reporting mechanic performance to the manager; and other duties as assigned.
15. If the Fleet Services Coordinator does not know the amount of time a certain repair job will take for a Fleet Services Mechanic, he or she can look it up in a book called a flat rate manual.
16. As with the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior, the Fleet Services Coordinator reports to the Support Services Manager.
17. The Fleet Services Coordinator has the authority to approve some overtime as needed. This authority is exercised when a mechanic needs some additional time to complete a repair or maintenance task at the end of the day. This amount averages six hours per month for all mechanics in toto.
18. To request vacation leave use, a Fleet Services Mechanic initially makes a request to the Fleet Services Coordinator, who reviews it for scheduling. The Fleet Services Coordinator then submits it to the Deputy Director for final approval with a recommendation.
19. Since the creation of the Fleet Services Coordinator position, no Fleet Services Mechanics have required discipline. However, it is anticipated that the Fleet Services Coordinator would generally be the first one to receive information and gather facts relating to a disciplinary issue. He or she would then report that to the Support Services Manager, who would report it up the chain of command. The actual discipline would be handed down by the Deputy Director. However, the Deputy Director may receive input from either the Fleet Services Coordinator or the Support Services Manager in making his or her disciplinary decision.
20. While the Fleet Services Coordinator cannot issue performance evaluations, he or she can use a computer program called “Quick Chats,” which is an employee performance information system. It allows employees to be tracked by supervisors up the chain of command and human resources. With Quick Chats, the Fleet Services Coordinator is able to make notes about employees’ performance. The Fleet Services Coordinator did not initially have access to Quick Chats when starting in July 2017. That access was provided approximately 90 days before the hearing in this case, which was after the filing of the Amended Petition. 6
21. The Fleet Services Coordinator has input into employee evaluations through Quick Chats and other means but does not complete them. They are completed by the Support Services Manager.
22. Previously when a grievance was filed by a Fleet Services Mechanic, it went to the Director.1 Additionally, the Support Services Manager believes that the Fleet Services Coordinator would have authority to allow a union steward to use on-duty time in processing a grievance.
23. The Fleet Services Coordinator cannot lay-off, transfer, demote or promote any of the Fleet Services Mechanics.
24. The Fleet Services Coordinator determines the training needs of the Fleet Services Mechanics. Prior to that position, the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior provided input on training, but did not have decision making authority.
25. Unlike the Fleet Services Mechanic Senior, the Fleet Services Coordinator can authorize in-house work warranty repairs.
26. At the time of the hearing in this case, there had not been any Fleet Services Mechanics hired since the Fleet Services Coordinator position was created. However, it is anticipated that the Fleet Services Coordinator’s role in the hiring process will be that he or she will participate in interviews as a panel member and provide input. The Fleet Service Mechanic Senior’s role was to create a practical test for mechanics – essentially by breaking something and seeing if the applicant could fix it. The Fleet Services Coordinator in position at the time of the hearing could not administer such a test and he is not a certified mechanic.
Procedural History
27. The City excluded the Fleet Services Coordinator from the bargaining unit. The City amended the Rules and Regulations Handbook for Non-represented Employees of the City of Medford to include the Fleet Services Coordinator as a non-represented confidential-professional employee, but did not include the position under supervisory personnel.
28. On September 18, 2017, the Petitioner filed a unit clarification, requesting that this Board clarify that the Fleet Services Coordinator was in the bargaining unit.
29. Following the Election Coordinator’s direction to amend the Oregon Administrative Rule under which the Petition was filed, the Petitioner filed an Amended Petition on October 18, 2017.
30. On November 8, 2017, the City filed objections asserting that the Fleet Services Coordinator is a supervisory employee, and therefore excluded from representation under ORS 243.650(23).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1The record was conflicting and unclear on how many grievances have been previously filed by Fleet Services Mechanics and how they were handled. 7
1. This Board has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this dispute.
2. The Fleet Services Coordinator is not a supervisor who is excluded from the bargaining unit by statute.
DISCUSSION
The issue in this case is whether the newly created position of Fleet Services Coordinator is in the bargaining unit. By statute, supervisors are not included in public employee bargaining units. To determine supervisory status, this Board assesses whether an employee meets the specific criteria set out in ORS 243.650(23), which defines a “supervisory employee” as:
“any individual having authority in the interest of the employer to hire, transfer, suspend, lay off, recall, promote, discharge, assign, reward or discipline other employees, or responsibly to direct them, or to adjust their grievances, or effectively recommend such action, if in connection therewith, the exercise of the authority is not of a merely routine or clerical nature but requires the use of independent judgment.”
Applying that definition, this Board has held that an employee’s supervisory status is established not by demonstrating the employee’s level of expertise or degree of responsibility, but by showing that the employee exercises “independent judgment” or “independent authority” in critical personnel matters. American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, Local 1085 v. State of Oregon Department of Justice, Case No. CC-003-10 at 31, 24 PECBR 893, 923 (2012).
Determining supervisory employee status requires the resolution of three questions, each of which must be answered in the affirmative for an employee to be deemed a supervisory employee: (1) does the employee have the authority to take action (or to effectively recommend action be taken) in any2 of the 12 listed activities; (2) does the exercise of that authority require the use of independent judgment; and (3) does the employee hold the authority in the interest of management. City of Portland v. Portland Police Commanding Officers Association, Case No. UC-017-13 at 22, 25 PECBR 996, 1017 (2014) (citing Deschutes County Sheriff’s Association v. Deschutes County, Case No. UC-62-94 at 12, 16 PECBR 328, 339 (1996)).
Hire/Fire/Lay-off/Recall
2In 1995, the legislature amended ORS 243.650(23) to eliminate the following sentence: “[h]owever, the exercise of any function of authority enumerated in this subsection shall not necessarily require the conclusion that the individual so exercising that function is a supervisor * * *.” The deletion of this sentence meant that the enumerated supervisory functions should be read in the disjunctive, which is how the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) had been interpreted by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) and federal courts. The result is that, if an otherwise “public employee” has authority under one of the twelve statutory criteria, the employee is a “supervisory employee” and not covered by the PECBA. City of Portland, UC-017-13 at 22, 25 PECBR at 1017.8
The Fleet Services Coordinator does not have independent authority with respect to hiring. His or her authority is limited to participation on an interview panel. We have previously held that participation as a member of a hiring panel – when the employee’s individual vote carries the same weight as other members of the panel – does not establish that a potential supervisor has the authority to effectively recommend the hiring of employees. City of Portland, UC-017-13 at 24, 25 PECBR at 1019. Further, the Fleet Services Coordinator does not have the authority to fire, lay-off, or recall employees. As such, the Fleet Services Coordinator position does not have independent authority with hiring, firing, lay-offs, or recalls.
Reward/Discipline/Suspend
The Fleet Services Coordinator does not have independent authority with respect to the ability to reward, discipline, or suspend. Given that customers and mechanics have frequent contact with the Fleet Services Coordinator, he or she would often be the first individual to observe performance, learn of a disciplinary issue, and would likely take on a fact finding role. The Fleet Services Coordinator may make a note in Quick Chats or otherwise communicate about the disciplinary issue with the Support Services Manager, who would report it up the chain of command. Ultimately, the actual discipline would be handed down by the Deputy Director.
Additionally, the City does not argue that the Fleet Services Coordinator’s use of the Quick Chats program is discipline. Accordingly, we do not analyze that question.
Transfer/Promote/Demote
The Fleet Services Coordinator does not have the ability to transfer, promote, or demote the Fleet Services Mechanics.
Assign
The City’s argument in favor of supporting supervisory status is that the Fleet Services Coordinator:
“schedules, plans, coordinates, and assigns repair and maintenance work amongst the Fleet Service’s Mechanics. The person in this position is responsible for deciding if overtime is necessary, without approval from a higher-level manager. The Fleet Services Coordinator is also responsible for determining work assignments for the Fleet Services Mechanics and how they work together as a team.” (Respondent’s Closing Brief, p. 5.)
The Petitioner responds that the statute does not contemplate this meaning of assign, quoting American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, Local 1085, UC-003-10 at 33, 24 PECBR at 925. In that case, we stated that:
“[u]nder the NLRA, an individual does not exercise the independent judgment expected of a supervisor if the individual bases assignment decisions on factors such as the employees’ skill and expertise, compatibility, and need to get particular projects accomplished. See Quadrex Environmental Company, Inc., 308 NLRB 101 (1992) (individuals are not supervisors where the assignment of work 9
‘demonstrates nothing more than the knowledge expected of experienced persons regarding which employees can perform particular tasks.’); Hexacomb Corporation and Western Temporary Services, Inc., 313 NLRB 983, 984 (1994) (foremen did not exercise independent judgment indicative of supervisory status ‘when they shift employees around within their respective lines to get projects accomplished.’); and Brown & Root, Inc., 314 NLRB 19, 21(1994) (an individual who makes assignments based on compatibility of employees and the skills needed to do particular jobs does not exercise independent judgment required of a supervisor).”
Two years later, in City of Portland, UC-017-13 at 26, 25 PECBR at 1021, we further examined the meaning of “assign” and more specifically defined it with respect to supervisory status. In that case, we referenced a more recent NLRB decision and adopted its reasoning. We quoted the following passage from Oakwood Healthcare, Inc., and International Union, United Automobile Aerospace and Agriculture Implement Workers of America, AFL-CIO, 348 NLRB 686, 688-89 (2006):
“‘The ordinary meaning of the term ‘assign’ is ‘to appoint to a post or duty.’ Webster’s Third New International Dictionary 132 (1981). Because this function shares with other [Section] 2(11) functions--i.e., hire, transfer, suspension, layoff, recall, promotion, discharge, reward, or discipline -- the common trait of affecting a term or condition of employment, we construe the term ‘assign’ to refer to the act of designating an employee to a place (such as a location, department, or wing), appointing an employee to a time (such as a shift or overtime period), or giving significant overall duties, i.e., tasks, to an employee. That is, the place, time, and work of an employee are part of his/her terms and conditions of employment. * * *
“The assignment of an employee to a certain department (e.g., housewares) or to a certain shift (e.g., night) or to certain significant overall tasks (e.g., restocking shelves) would generally qualify as ‘assign’ within our construction. However, choosing the order in which the employee will perform discrete tasks within those assignments (e.g., restocking toasters before coffeemakers) would not be indicative of exercising the authority to ‘assign.’ * * * In sum, to ‘assign’ for purposes of Section 2(11) refers to the * * * designation of significant overall duties to an employee, not to the * * * instruction that the employee perform a discrete task.’”
Since then we have concisely defined “assign” to mean “the act of designating an employee to a place (such as a location, department, or wing), appointing an employee to a time (such as a shift or overtime period), or giving significant overall duties, i.e., tasks, to an employee.” Hillsboro Sergeant’s Association v. City of Hillsboro, Oregon, Case No. CC-009-14 at 26, 26 PECBR 491, 495 (2015) (quoting City of Portland, UC-017-13 at 26, 25 PECBR at 1021 (quoting Oakwood Healthcare, Inc., and International Union, United Automobile Aerospace and Agriculture Implement Workers of America, AFL-CIO, 348 NLRB 686, 689 (2006)).
The Fleet Services Coordinator does not determine the Fleet Service Mechanics’ general shifts, home base location, or overall duties. Rather, the Fleet Service Coordinator dispatches the Fleet Services Mechanics to complete discrete tasks – i.e., maintenance and repair of specific equipment and vehicles – and he or she determines the orders in which they will perform them. 10
These decisions are based on factors such as the employees’ skill and expertise, compatibility, and need to get particular projects accomplished.
The Fleet Services Coordinator does have authority to grant some degree of overtime. However, this is a small amount, totaling just about six hours a month for all of the Fleet Service Mechanics. This is only provided in order to allow them to finish jobs at the end of a shift which are nearly complete. This is distinct from a situation where a supervisor would determine the overall operational needs of a department or agency and assign overtime to individuals as a management strategy. As such, we conclude that the Fleet Services Coordinator does not “assign” as meant by the statute.
Direct
Along with “assign,” we also examined the meaning of “to direct” in City of Portland, UC-017-13 at 1, 25 PECBR at 996. We concluded that a determination that an employee has a “responsibly to direct” requires that a putative supervisor must be accountable (such that some adverse consequence may befall the supervisor) if the employees that they allegedly direct fail to adequately perform their duties. As with the meaning of “assign,” we also relied on Oakwood Healthcare, Inc., 348 NLRB at 691-92, in our analysis. In that case, the NLRB concluded that:
“Thus, to establish accountability for purposes of responsible direction, it must be shown that the employer delegated to the putative supervisor the authority to direct the work and the authority to take corrective action, if necessary. It also must be shown that there is a prospect of adverse consequences for the putative supervisor if he/she does not take these steps.” Id. at 691-692.
In this case, there is no evidence in the record that the Fleet Services Coordinator is at risk of suffering adverse consequences if a Fleet Services Mechanic fails to satisfactorily complete his or her duties. Accordingly, we can conclude that he or she does not have authority “to direct” as meant by ORS 243.650(23).
Adjust Grievances
There is no evidence in the record to suggest that the Fleet Services Coordinator would have the ability to adjust grievances of the Fleet Services Mechanics. At hearing, there was limited testimony about a grievance that was previously filed. In that case, it was filed with the Director of Public Services. Otherwise, the record was unclear about grievance filing in Fleet Services.
Performance Evaluations
Although an employee’s role in evaluating other employees is not one of the criteria listed in ORS 243.650(23), the ability to do so may directly affect the hiring and disciplinary process, and “‘we consider it to the extent it constitutes evidence that [the employee] effectively recommends personnel action.’” Laborers’ International of North America, Local 483, Law Enforcement Professional Association v. City of Gervais, Case No. UC-16-08 at 19, 23 PECBR 143, 161 (2009) (quoting City of Union v. Laborers’ International Union of North America, Local 121, Case No. UC-09-08, 22 PECBR 872, 886 (2008) citing Deschutes County Sheriff's Association v. Deschutes County, Case No. UC-62-94, 16 PECBR 328, 341 (1996)).11
The Fleet Services Coordinator does not complete performance evaluations for the Fleet Services Mechanics. He or she provides input on their performance through Quick Chats and other means, but the Support Services Manager ultimately has responsibility for completing the Fleet Service Mechanic’s performance evaluations.
Summary
Based on the above, we conclude that the Fleet Services Coordinator is not excluded from the bargaining unit as a supervisor. There is no evidence that the Fleet Services Coordinator exercises independent judgment or independent authority in hiring, transferring, suspending, laying off, recalling, promoting, discharging, assigning, rewarding, or disciplining other employees, or the responsibly to direct them, or to adjust their grievances.
3. The Fleet Services Coordinator is included in the bargaining unit based on the
Agreement.
The Petitioner argues that “[b]y its terms the recognition clause automatically incorporates all new classifications within the Fleet Services Department that are not excluded. The FSC position is not ‘part-time, temporary, supervisory [or] confidential.’ Therefore the FSC position is included in the bargaining unit under the express terms of the collective bargaining agreement.” (Petitioner’s Closing Brief, p. 17).
The parties’ Agreement states:
“2.1 Recognition - The City recognizes Teamsters Local Union No. 223 as the exclusive bargaining agent for all non-excluded employees in covered classifications in the Public Works Department. Classifications in the bargaining unit include Auto Service Worker, Fleet Services Mechanic and Fleet Services Mechanic Senior.
2.2 Excluded Employees - Part-time, temporary, supervisory and confidential employees are excluded from the bargaining unit. Part-time employees are those who work less than forty (40) hours per week. Temporary employees are those who are hired for a limited period of time not to exceed six (6) consecutive months from date of employment in a twelve (12) month period.
2.3 New Classifications - The City has the exclusive right to develop new classifications within the current organizational scope of this bargaining unit and adopt wage scales for those classifications. The City shall forward the new position classification specification and hourly wage schedule to the Union for its review. If the Union disagrees with the proposed wage scale for this new classification, the Union may reopen this Agreement for negotiations of only that new hourly wage scale for that new classification under the scope of this Agreement.” (Exh. R-1 at 5.)
The Agreement includes specific positions in the bargaining unit, of which the Fleet Services Coordinator is not included because it did not exist when the Agreement was negotiated. This language allows the City to create new classifications within the bargaining unit, but the City 12
intended to create one outside of it. Although we have determined that it is statutorily included in the unit, this does not mean the City acted in violation of the Agreement. However, as we have concluded that the Fleet Services Coordinator is not supervisory, it would be included by the language of the Agreement.
PROPOSED ORDER
The Fleet Services Coordinator is included in the Petitioner’s bargaining unit.
SIGNED AND ISSUED on July 20, 2018.
_________________________________________
JULIE D. READING
Administrative Law Judge
